text: Which 1956 summer workshop is widely considered the founding event of artificial intelligence as a field?
explanation: John McCarthy, Marvin Minsky, Nathaniel Rochester and Claude Shannon wrote the proposal that started it, and McCarthy picked the name artificial intelligence while doing so. The workshop is often called the constitutional convention of AI, and the 1956 date is the field's accepted starting line.
answerAliases: Dartmouth Summer Research Project on Artificial Intelligence

text: Which researcher coined the term "artificial intelligence" while writing the proposal for the 1956 workshop?
explanation: McCarthy (1927 to 2011) is usually given the credit, on the grounds that he chose the name to avoid the baggage of cybernetics. He also led the development of Lisp, which became the working language of AI research for two decades.

text: Which American psychologist built the perceptron, the first trainable artificial neural network?
explanation: Rosenblatt built it at Cornell in the late 1950s and described it in 1958, and the idea was simple enough that IBM built a machine to run it. He was killed in a boating accident in 1971, a few years before the field's second winter had finished.

text: Which MIT researcher wrote ELIZA between 1964 and 1967, the program most often credited as the first chatbot?
explanation: ELIZA matched patterns and substituted phrases, with no understanding of what was said underneath. Weizenbaum was disturbed by how much his colleagues opened up to it, which turned into an influential argument that the illusion of understanding is not the same thing as understanding.

text: Which IBM researcher coined the term "machine learning" in 1959?
explanation: Samuel was writing a checkers program and defined learning as getting better at a task without being explicitly programmed to. The checkers player was among the first self-improving programs, and the definition has aged extremely well.

text: In the history of AI, what does the term "AI winter" refer to?
options: A period when datasets were withdrawn from public use
A period when funding and interest in AI research collapsed
A period when neural networks replaced symbolic systems
A period when computers became too small to train models
answer: A period when funding and interest in AI research collapsed
explanation: The field has gone through several hype cycles, each one followed by disappointment, criticism and funding cuts, and then a revival years later. There were two major winters, roughly in the mid 1970s and again after the expert systems bust in the late 1980s.
answerAliases: a period of reduced funding and interest in AI research

text: Which long-running project set out to encode common sense knowledge as an explicit ontology?
explanation: Cyc started at MCC in July 1984 and later became Cycorp, and it is still running. The bet was that a machine needs hand-encoded facts about how the world works before it can reason at all, which is a much larger bet than the one deep learning eventually won.

text: Which programming language did John McCarthy develop, and did it become the standard language of early AI research?
explanation: McCarthy designed Lisp at MIT in the late 1950s and it became the lingua franca of AI for about twenty years. Its garbage collector, its trees and its interactive REPL all existed for the convenience of people experimenting with symbolic programs, and most of what feels modern about Lisp tooling descends from it.

text: MYCIN diagnosed blood infections and recommended antibiotics. What kind of system was it?
options: An early backward chaining expert system
An early case based reasoning shell
answer: An early backward chaining expert system
explanation: MYCIN worked backward from a suspected infection through rules of the form if this, then that, using a small weighted certainty scheme rather than probabilities. It was genuinely good, the name comes from the -mycin suffix on the antibiotics it recommended, and it never shipped because nobody could work out who was liable when it was wrong.

text: In 1997, Deep Blue became the first computer to win a match against a reigning world champion. Who was the champion?
explanation: Kasparov had held the title since 1985 and had a peak rating of 2851, the highest ever recorded at the time. Deep Blue won a six game match in three and a half hours, and the rematch the following year ended in a draw, which is the fairest summary of how close it actually was.

text: The 1956 workshop that launched AI as a field was hosted by which college?
explanation: The Dartmouth Summer Research Project was held at Dartmouth College in Hanover, New Hampshire. MIT and Stanford are tempting because both became major AI centers later, but neither hosted the 1956 workshop.

text: Before Deep Blue, IBM's chess computer was known by which name?
explanation: Deep Thought was developed at Carnegie Mellon and later at IBM, and it was the direct predecessor of Deep Blue. ChipTest was an even earlier machine from the same lineage, which is why it tempts people who know the story but not the order.

text: In which year did Garry Kasparov and Deep Blue play their first six-game match?
explanation: The first match was played in Philadelphia in February 1996, and Kasparov won it 4 to 2. 1997 is the year of the rematch that Deep Blue won, which is the result most people remember.

text: Where was the 1997 rematch between Deep Blue and Garry Kasparov held?
explanation: The rematch took place at the Equitable Center in New York City in May 1997, and Deep Blue won 3.5 to 2.5. Philadelphia hosted the first match in 1996, which is the mix-up the question is built on.

source.title: Deep Blue versus Garry Kasparov
source.label: Deep Blue versus Garry Kasparov on Wikipedia

text: After which game of the 1997 rematch did Kasparov accuse IBM of cheating?
explanation: Kasparov made the accusation after Game 2, whose move 37 (Be4) he thought was too sophisticated for a machine. IBM denied any human intervention, and Kasparov later said he had overreacted.

source.title: Deep Blue versus Garry Kasparov
source.label: Deep Blue versus Garry Kasparov on Wikipedia

text: Which two human champions did IBM Watson defeat on Jeopardy in 2011?
explanation: Watson beat Ken Jennings and Brad Rutter in February 2011. The chess and Go names are the usual cross-sport confusion, since both are famous human-versus-machine matches but from different games.

text: IBM's Watson system, which won Jeopardy in 2011, was named after whom?
explanation: Watson is named after Thomas J. Watson, IBM's founder, not after the scientist. Alan Turing and Claude Shannon are tempting because they are famous computing pioneers, but neither gave the system its name.

text: In what year did Fei-Fei Li begin building the ImageNet dataset?
explanation: Li started ImageNet in 2007, and the paper presenting it appeared in 2009. 2009 and 2012 are the years people most often confuse with the start, because those are when the dataset and the famous competition results were published.

text: Which neural network's 2012 victory in the ImageNet competition is often cited as the start of the deep learning boom?
explanation: AlexNet won the ImageNet challenge in 2012 with a top-5 error far below the runner-up, and Yann LeCun called it an unequivocal turning point. ResNet and VGG came later and improved on it, which is why they tempt people who know the timeline only loosely.

text: Who introduced generative adversarial networks (GANs) in 2014?
explanation: Goodfellow introduced GANs in a 2014 paper written with colleagues at the Universite de Montreal. Hinton, LeCun and Bengio are the tempting wrong answers because they are the other famous deep learning pioneers of the same era.

text: Where was the 2016 match in which AlphaGo defeated Lee Sedol held?
explanation: AlphaGo beat Lee Sedol 4 to 1 in Seoul in March 2016. Beijing is the tempting miss because DeepMind later played Ke Jie there, but the Lee Sedol match was in Seoul.

text: In which year did OpenAI release GPT-3?
explanation: GPT-3 was released in 2020 with 175 billion parameters, a hundred times larger than GPT-2. 2019 is the GPT-2 year and 2021 is when DALL-E arrived, which is why both tempt people.

text: Which model family underpinned ChatGPT at its November 2022 launch?
explanation: ChatGPT launched on top of a GPT-3.5 fine-tune, not a new frontier model. GPT-4 arrived in March 2023, which is why people often assume it was there from the start.

text: Which technique did OpenAI describe in its 2022 InstructGPT work for making language models follow instructions?
explanation: InstructGPT used reinforcement learning from human feedback to train a smaller model that humans preferred over the much larger GPT-3. Constitutional AI is Anthropic's separate method, which is the confusion the distractor is built on.

source.title: Reinforcement learning from human feedback
source.label: Reinforcement learning from human feedback on Wikipedia

text: In which month and year did Anthropic publish the Constitutional AI paper?
explanation: Anthropic published Constitutional AI in December 2022 as a method for training a harmless assistant from a written constitution plus AI feedback. June 2023 is when Claude became publicly available, which is the mix-up the distractor targets.

text: Which 2020 paper popularized denoising diffusion probabilistic models for image generation?
options: Denoising Diffusion Probabilistic Models (Ho et al.)
answer: Denoising Diffusion Probabilistic Models (Ho et al.)
explanation: Jonathan Ho, Ajay Jain and Pieter Abbeel published DDPM in 2020, which is what made diffusion models practical for images. The GAN option is the technique diffusion displaced, and Attention Is All You Need is the transformer paper, so neither fits.

text: In which year did OpenAI first announce DALL-E?
explanation: OpenAI revealed DALL-E in a blog post on January 5, 2021, using a modified GPT-3 to generate images from text. 2022 is when DALL-E 2 arrived, which is the mix-up the distractor targets.

text: In which year did Midjourney enter open beta?
explanation: Midjourney entered open beta on July 12, 2022, and the company was already profitable by its August 2022 open beta. 2023 is the year of its V5 release, which is the confusion the distractor targets.

text: The first global AI Safety Summit in November 2023 was hosted at which historic site?
explanation: The UK hosted the first global AI Safety Summit at Bletchley Park, the wartime codebreaking site, on November 1 and 2, 2023. It produced the Bletchley Declaration signed by 28 countries. Windsor Castle is the tempting distractor because it is another famous British site.

text: Which city hosted the second global AI Safety Summit in May 2024?
explanation: The AI Seoul Summit in May 2024 was co-hosted by South Korea and the UK, following the 2023 Bletchley Park summit. Paris hosted the 2025 AI Action Summit, which is the mix-up the distractor targets.

text: In which year did the European Parliament adopt the EU AI Act?
explanation: MEPs adopted the EU AI Act on March 13, 2024, and it entered into force on August 1, 2024. 2023 is when the European Parliament reached its negotiating position, which is the mix-up the distractor targets.

text: The Asilomar AI Principles were published in which year?
explanation: The Future of Life Institute sponsored the Asilomar Conference on Beneficial AI in January 2017, where more than 100 leaders formulated 23 principles for beneficial AI. 2015 is the year the open letter on autonomous weapons was published, which is the mix-up the distractor targets.

source.title: Asilomar Conference on Beneficial AI
source.label: Asilomar Conference on Beneficial AI on Wikipedia

text: In which city was DeepMind founded in 2010?
explanation: DeepMind was founded in London in 2010 by Demis Hassabis, Shane Legg and Mustafa Suleyman. Mountain View is where Google is headquartered, which is the mix-up the distractor targets.

text: In which year did Google acquire DeepMind?
explanation: Google acquired DeepMind in 2014 for a reported 400 to 650 million dollars. 2016 is when AlphaGo beat Lee Sedol, which is the event people most often confuse with the acquisition year.

text: In which year was Anthropic founded?
explanation: Dario and Daniela Amodei founded Anthropic in 2021 after leaving OpenAI. 2022 is when Claude was trained and the Constitutional AI paper appeared, which is the mix-up the distractor targets.

text: In which year was Hugging Face founded?
explanation: Hugging Face was founded in New York in 2016 as a chatbot for teenagers and later pivoted into the model hub. 2018 is when it open-sourced the model behind its chatbot, which is the mix-up the distractor targets.

text: At which university was AlexNet developed?
explanation: Alex Krizhevsky, Ilya Sutskever and Geoffrey Hinton built AlexNet at the University of Toronto. Stanford is the tempting miss because Fei-Fei Li, who created ImageNet, is based there.

text: In which year did Frank Rosenblatt first describe the perceptron?
explanation: Rosenblatt described the perceptron in 1958 while at Cornell, and IBM built a machine to run it. 1969 is the year of the Minsky and Papert book that criticized it, which is the mix-up the distractor targets.

text: What was the name of ELIZA's most famous script that simulated a Rogerian psychotherapist?
explanation: ELIZA's best-known script was called DOCTOR, which echoed user statements back as questions in the style of a Rogerian therapist. PARRY and SHRDLU are other classic programs, which is why they tempt people who know the era but not the names.

text: Which program did Terry Winograd create in 1970 to demonstrate natural language understanding in a blocks world?
explanation: Winograd built SHRDLU at MIT in 1970 to manipulate blocks in a virtual world using natural language. ELIZA is the chatbot from the same era, which is why it tempts people who know the period but not the specific program.

text: In which year did the Cyc project begin?
explanation: Cyc started at MCC in July 1984 and later became Cycorp, and it is still running. 1990 is when the company was spun out, which is the mix-up the distractor targets.

text: Which 1973 report criticized AI progress and contributed to the first AI winter in the UK?
explanation: James Lighthill's 1973 survey, now called the Lighthill report, criticized AI's failure to achieve its grandiose objectives and helped trigger funding cuts. The other reports are plausible-sounding inventions, which is why the question tests whether you know the actual name.

text: Which country launched the Fifth Generation Computer Systems project in the 1980s?
explanation: Japan's Ministry of International Trade and Industry launched the Fifth Generation Computer Systems project in 1982 to develop parallel computers and logic programming. The United States is the tempting miss because it funded most other AI research of the era.

source.title: Fifth Generation Computer Systems
source.label: Fifth Generation Computer Systems on Wikipedia

text: Which company's expert system XCON configured computer orders and became a famous AI success of the 1980s?
explanation: XCON, originally called R1, was built at Carnegie Mellon for Digital Equipment Corporation to configure computer orders, and it became the canonical expert-system success story. IBM is the tempting miss because it built most other famous AI systems of the era.

text: Which 1986 paper popularized backpropagation for training neural networks?
options: Playing Atari with Deep Reinforcement Learning
explanation: Rumelhart, Hinton and Williams published Learning representations by back-propagating errors in Nature in 1986 and popularized the algorithm. Attention Is All You Need is the transformer paper, which is why it tempts people who know the modern era but not the 1980s.

text: In November 2020, AlphaFold 2 won which competition by a wide margin?
explanation: AlphaFold 2 won CASP14 in November 2020, scoring above 90 on the global distance test for about two-thirds of proteins. CASP13 is the previous competition where AlphaFold 1 placed first but far less impressively, which is the mix-up the distractor targets.

text: In which 1950 paper did Alan Turing propose the imitation game?
options: Systems of Logic Based on Ordinals
explanation: Turing's 1950 paper Computing Machinery and Intelligence introduced the imitation game that became known as the Turing test. On Computable Numbers is his 1936 paper on computability, which is the tempting wrong answer for people who know Turing but not the AI paper.

source.title: Computing Machinery and Intelligence
source.label: Computing Machinery and Intelligence on Wikipedia

text: In which year did McCulloch and Pitts publish their mathematical model of a neuron?
explanation: Warren McCulloch and Walter Pitts published A Logical Calculus of the Ideas Immanent in Nervous Activity in 1943, the first mathematical model of a neuron. 1956 is the Dartmouth year, which is the mix-up the distractor targets.

text: Which 1969 book by Marvin Minsky and Seymour Papert criticized single-layer perceptrons and contributed to the first AI winter?
explanation: Minsky and Papert's 1969 book Perceptrons showed the limitations of single-layer perceptrons and is often blamed for chilling neural network research for a decade. The Society of Mind and The Emotion Machine are Minsky's later books, which is why they tempt people who know the author but not the title.
answerAliases: Perceptrons: An Introduction to Computational Geometry

text: Which company, founded in 1980, became the leading maker of Lisp machines in the 1980s?
explanation: Symbolics was spun out of the MIT AI Lab and became the leading maker of Lisp machines in the 1980s. Xerox is the tempting miss because it also built Lisp workstations, but Symbolics was the dominant vendor.

text: Which university developed MYCIN in the 1970s?
explanation: MYCIN was developed over five or six years in the early 1970s at Stanford University. MIT is the tempting miss because ELIZA and SHRDLU came from there, but MYCIN was Stanford's.

text: Which expert system, developed at Stanford in the 1960s, identified molecular structures from mass spectra?
explanation: DENDRAL, built at Stanford in the 1960s, was the first expert system and identified molecular structures from mass spectrometry data. MYCIN is the tempting miss because it is the other famous Stanford expert system, but it diagnosed blood infections instead.

text: Which robot, built at SRI in the late 1960s, was the first mobile robot to reason about its own actions?
explanation: Shakey was built at SRI International from 1966 to 1972 and was the first general-purpose mobile robot able to reason about its own actions. ASIMO and BigDog are much later robots, which is why they tempt people who know robotics but not the history.

text: Which 1989 Carnegie Mellon project trained a neural network to drive a vehicle autonomously?
explanation: ALVINN, an Autonomous Land Vehicle in a Neural Network, was developed by Dean Pomerleau at Carnegie Mellon in 1989 and drove at up to 19 miles per hour. Stanley, Boss and Junior are later Darpa Grand Challenge vehicles, which is why they tempt people who know self-driving history but not the 1980s.
answerAliases: Autonomous Land Vehicle in a Neural Network

text: Which four-legged robot, developed by Boston Dynamics in 2005, became an internet sensation?
explanation: Boston Dynamics developed BigDog in 2005, and its uncanny walking videos made it an early internet sensation. Spot and Atlas are later Boston Dynamics robots, which is why they tempt people who know the company but not the dates.

text: Which humanoid robot did Honda unveil in 2000?
explanation: Honda unveiled ASIMO in 2000 as a humanoid robot that could walk and climb stairs. Atlas and Pepper are later robots from Boston Dynamics and SoftBank, which is why they tempt people who know humanoid robots but not the dates.

text: In which year did IBM's Watson compete on Jeopardy?
explanation: Watson competed on Jeopardy in February 2011 against Ken Jennings and Brad Rutter. 2009 is when the system was first demonstrated internally, which is the mix-up the distractor targets.

text: In which year was the ImageNet dataset first published?
explanation: The ImageNet paper was presented at CVPR in 2009, although Fei-Fei Li began building it in 2007. 2012 is when AlexNet won the competition, which is the mix-up the distractor targets.

text: In which year did Ian Goodfellow introduce GANs?
explanation: Goodfellow introduced GANs in a 2014 paper, and the idea spread quickly through image generation research. 2012 is the AlexNet year, which is the mix-up the distractor targets.

text: At which conference was Attention Is All You Need presented in 2017?
explanation: The paper was presented at the 31st Conference on Neural Information Processing Systems (NeurIPS) in 2017. ICLR is the tempting miss because many transformer follow-ups appeared there, but the original was at NeurIPS.

source.label: Attention Is All You Need on NeurIPS

text: DeepMind released WaveNet, which generates raw audio waveforms, in which year?
explanation: DeepMind released WaveNet in September 2016, showing that deep learning could model raw audio directly. 2018 is the tempting answer because Tacotron 2 arrived then, but WaveNet itself dates to 2016.

text: Who published the first neural style transfer paper in 2015?
explanation: Leon Gatys and colleagues released 'A Neural Algorithm of Artistic Style' on arXiv in 2015, applying a trained convolutional network to repaint photos in another image's style. Ian Goodfellow is the tempting answer as another famous generative-AI pioneer, but GANs are his, not style transfer.
answerAliases: A Neural Algorithm of Artistic Style

text: Which open-source project launched in March 2023 kicked off the autonomous-agent craze?
explanation: AutoGPT, released in March 2023, let a GPT-4 model loop over its own outputs and tool calls with no human in the loop, which is what started the agent gold rush. LangChain is the tempting answer as the most-used agent framework, but it is a library, not the project that sparked the craze.

text: OpenAI announced GPT-4 in which month of 2023?
explanation: OpenAI announced GPT-4 on March 14, 2023, and it powered the paid tier of ChatGPT from launch. January is the tempting answer because ChatGPT itself had just gone viral, but GPT-4 came two months later.

text: Google announced Bard in which month of 2023?
explanation: Google announced Bard on February 6, 2023, the week before Microsoft's Bing Chat event, as a direct response to ChatGPT. April is the tempting answer because that is when early access opened, but the announcement came in February.

text: In which year did Meta release the first LLaMA model?
explanation: Meta released LLaMA on February 24, 2023, initially to researchers under a non-commercial license. 2022 is the tempting answer because that was the ChatGPT shockwave year, but LLaMA came the following February.

text: DeepMind's AlphaStar beat professional players at which game?
explanation: AlphaStar defeated professional StarCraft II players in 2019 using a multi-agent reinforcement learning setup. Dota 2 is the tempting answer because OpenAI Five played that game the same year, but AlphaStar's game was StarCraft.

text: Which DeepMind model learned to plan without knowing the rules of the game?
explanation: MuZero, published in 2019, learned its own model of the environment and planned with it, mastering Go, chess, shogi and Atari without being given the rules. AlphaZero is the tempting answer because it also masters games from scratch, but it was given the rules.

text: OpenAI Five competed in which esport?
explanation: OpenAI Five played Dota 2 and beat the reigning world champions OG in 2019. StarCraft II is the tempting answer because AlphaStar played that the same year, but OpenAI Five's game was Dota.

text: Which 2022 DeepMind study argued that models were undertrained relative to data?
explanation: DeepMind's Chinchilla paper in March 2022 argued that for a given compute budget, smaller models trained on more data outperform larger ones trained on less. PaLM is the tempting answer as another 2022 DeepMind model, but PaLM was the large model Chinchilla critiqued.
